One project can have two internal rates of return: keep the later payment in the picture

Three charts follow an initial outlay, a later receipt and a final obligation, then reveal why the same cash flows can have more than one nonnegative IRR.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Keep the later obligation in the cash flows before solving for a return

Interactive planning lab

NPV at the selected annual discount assumption$18.9
Distinct nonnegative annual IRRs10.00% and 20.00%
Undiscounted sum of all three cash flows-$200

Original three-date project illustration: an outflow immediately, an inflow exactly one year later, and a required outflow exactly two years later. Cash flows are independently entered nominal CAD and contain no taxes, financing, interim deposits, bank balances or additional terminal value. The NPV input is an effective annual discount assumption, not a promised yield or an automatically suitable hurdle rate. IRRs are mathematical roots of NPV = 0. The solver lists distinct finite roots at or above 0% only; any negative roots are outside the stated domain. A repeated root is listed once. The profile shows 0% to the greater of 30% and the selected discount input, so an admissible root beyond that range can be listed in the metric without appearing in the plot. No reinvestment or final household wealth is calculated. A later obligation remains payable regardless of how much of the earlier receipt has been spent.

The central idea

An IRR is a discount rate that makes a cash-flow valuation equal zero. With a later outflow, there may be several such rates, so read the dated cash flows and NPV profile before relying on one percentage.

01

Put the final obligation on the timeline

A project can require cash now, return cash later and still leave another payment due. Ending an analysis at the first receipt can hide that obligation and turn a partial cash-flow record into an apparently attractive return.

The original example pays CAD 10,000 immediately, receives CAD 23,000 at the end of year one, and requires CAD 13,200 at the end of year two. The last amount could represent an independently estimated closing or restoration obligation in a hypothetical project. It is entered as a required payment rather than treated as an optional use of profit.

The first chart shows the signs from the participant’s perspective: negative, positive, negative. A payment and a receipt one year apart cannot simply be netted as though they occur on the same date. That separation matters to both valuation and the eventual cash required.

No actual project, security or contract is being offered. The amounts are fixed teaching assumptions, with no claim that the receipt or final bill is certain in real life. A practical review would need complete cash-flow evidence, taxes, financing conditions, risk and other obligations.

02

NPV values all the flows at one stated discount assumption

Net present value converts future flows to a common starting date. For an effective annual discount assumption r, this example uses −10,000 + 23,000 ÷ (1 + r) − 13,200 ÷ (1 + r)2.

At 15%, the year-one receipt has a present value of CAD 20,000. The year-two payment has a present value of approximately CAD 9,981.10. Subtracting the immediate CAD 10,000 payment leaves NPV of approximately CAD 18.90.

The waterfall displays those three components separately. The small positive endpoint means the modeled discounted receipt exceeds the modeled discounted payments by that amount at the selected assumption. It is not a cash account holding CAD 18.90 or a guarantee that the project can pay its last bill.

The undiscounted sum is negative CAD 200. That different result uses no time adjustment. Neither measure should be relabeled as the other. OpenStax’s NPV discussion provides the general valuation framework; all amounts and calculations in this article are independently authored.

03

IRR solves for a zero valuation instead of accepting a discount input

An internal rate of return is a rate at which the NPV equation equals zero. For the original cash flows, 10% is one solution: the CAD 23,000 receipt discounted one year and the CAD 13,200 payment discounted two years exactly reconcile with the initial outlay.

But 20% also makes the same equation zero. The cash-flow pattern therefore has two distinct nonnegative annual IRRs. Reporting only whichever rate a trial-and-error routine happens to find would conceal another mathematical solution.

The reason can be checked algebraically. Let g = 1 + r. Multiplying the zero-NPV equation by g squared gives 10,000g2 − 23,000g + 13,200 = 0. It factors into growth factors of 1.10 and 1.20, corresponding to the two rates.

The rate metric solves that quadratic directly. It does not search only the plotted grid or treat two adjacent plotted values as proof that a unique rate exists. Depending on the entered flows, the stated nonnegative domain can contain zero, one or two distinct rates.

04

The NPV profile explains why one higher-rate rule can fail

The line chart evaluates the entire three-flow NPV at a range of annual discount assumptions. In the original example, NPV is negative at 0%, zero at 10%, positive around 15%, zero again at 20%, and negative beyond the upper root.

The later payment is discounted for two years while the receipt is discounted for one. Raising the rate reduces the present value of both. Their competing effects mean the total need not fall continuously as the rate rises. A rule learned for an initial outflow followed only by inflows cannot be applied automatically to every sign-changing pattern.

OpenStax’s IRR discussion identifies multiple mathematical solutions as a limitation when later negative flows occur. This article uses that mathematical fact to inspect one original example; it does not turn the higher root into a superior choice or recommend a discount rate.

The profile starts at 0% and extends to at least 30%. If the selected discount input is higher, it extends to that input. A listed root beyond the visible range remains a root even though the line chart does not show it. The metric states that only nonnegative rates are listed; a negative solution is outside this guide’s chosen domain.

05

A repeated root and no admissible root are meaningful outcomes

Change the final payment to CAD 13,225 while retaining the original initial cost and receipt. The two growth-factor roots meet at 1.15. The solver lists a single distinct 15% rate, and the NPV curve touches zero there rather than crossing into a positive region.

This is why counting visible crossings is insufficient. A tangent zero is still a mathematical solution. A repeated solution should also not be presented as two different rates merely because a quadratic formula returns it twice.

Other entries can produce no nonnegative solution. A positive year-two obligation with too little earlier receipt may leave NPV below zero for every nonnegative discount rate. If the final payment is zero, the remaining two-date problem can instead have one nonnegative IRR, depending on the receipt relative to the initial outlay.

Scaling every cash amount by the same positive factor leaves the roots unchanged while scaling NPV by that factor. A percentage therefore does not measure the dollar size of a project’s value or funding requirement. Two opportunities with equal rate roots can still place very different amounts of household money at risk.

06

Add the cash plan before interpreting a return

The year-one receipt is not automatically available for unrestricted spending. In the original example, a required payment remains due one year later. The household needs a supported plan for that date even when a valuation metric is positive.

This calculator does not hold the receipt in an account, assign it a reinvestment rate or compute final wealth. It also does not obtain credit for a later shortfall. A dated cash plan would separately identify available starting resources, what happens to the receipt, and how the final payment is funded.

The discount input is an assumption used for valuation. Selecting a higher number does not make a project safer, increase its actual receipts or remove an obligation. The appropriate treatment of risk and the comparison with other uses of money require facts beyond these three entered flows.

Use the charts to check completeness before relying on a quoted percentage. Keep every material inflow and outflow at its own date, inspect whether more than one admissible rate exists, and read NPV at explicitly supported assumptions. Then evaluate the actual contract, uncertainty and payment capacity as part of the wider decision.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All cash flows and discount assumptions are original hypothetical examples. The three-date pattern is deliberately limited. The solver lists distinct finite nonnegative IRRs only and does not value an actual investment, calculate reinvestment or establish payment feasibility. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
